title: Rehras with others
hook: a household that prays Rehras together hears the day end the same way

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhiaa, dusk as a practice, and your line, put the day down. Did you keep one moment that ended the workday? Today, the same evening prayer, said with other people. Day four hundred nineteen.

Seven-thirty in the evening, a small house in Birmingham. A father props his phone against the fruit bowl. On the screen: his sister in Toronto, still at her kitchen counter in the afternoon light, and her two kids squeezed into the frame. He starts: so dar keha. His sister joins on the second line. The kids murmur, then catch up by the Chaupai. Two cities, two clocks, one Rehras. Today: Rehras with others.
screen: `A PHONE PROPPED ON THE FRUIT BOWL.` → `BIRMINGHAM AND TORONTO, ONE SCREEN.` → `TWO CLOCKS, ONE REHRAS.`

segments.voice: Rehras can be said alone, on a train, under your breath. It's also said together: a household in the front room, a congregation in the gurdwara in the evening, cousins on a video call across continents. Why does that matter? Gurbani puts a lot of weight on sangat, the company of people who remember the One. Guru Nanak asks, in Sri Raag, how the true congregation is to be recognized, and answers, in paraphrase: it's where the One Name is spoken. Not where the building is grandest. Where the Name is. You've heard this all through Rehras. Guru Nanak, stuck in the mud, sought the shelter of those who remember. Guru Arjan said join the company of the holy, and that whoever meets the true congregation is carried across. Rehras keeps pointing at other people. There's also something simpler. When a household says Rehras together, the children hear it before they can read it. They learn where the pauses fall, which lines the grandmother says slowly, when everyone stands for Ardas. A day that ends the same way for everyone in a house gives the house a shared clock. Even when the day went badly, even after an argument at dinner, everyone hears the same words: joy has come, mother; protect me with your hand; may all be well. Saying it together doesn't erase the argument. But it's hard to stay quite as far apart after you've stood side by side for Ardas. End the day together.
screen: `ALONE, OR TOGETHER: HOME, GURDWARA, SCREEN.` · `SANGAT: WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · `REHRAS KEEPS POINTING AT OTHER PEOPLE.` · `A HOUSE WITH A SHARED CLOCK.` · then, large: `END THE DAY TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invite one person to join. Think of someone you could end a day with: a partner, a child, a parent, a friend who lives far away. It doesn't have to be the whole of Rehras. It might be two lines of the Chaupai, or one minute of quiet together, or just a shared thank you. Picture asking them. Picture what it would be like to end tonight side by side, even by phone. Hold that picture and breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, for them. The bell holds the time.
Rehras with others. The evening prayer said together, at home, in the gurdwara or across a screen, so a household and a sangat hear the day end the same way.
Your line: end the day together. Tonight, ask one person to share one minute with you at day's end: a line, a quiet, a thank you. Day four hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Rehras Sahib is recited in the evening in gurdwaras with the sangat, and families often say it together at home, one person often leading, ending with Ardas said standing; some families now join by phone or video across cities.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sangat, the congregation, the company of those who remember the One.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rehras with others just means a group recitation.
what it means: ending the day in sangat, so a household shares one clock and children learn the prayer by hearing it.
what a scholar hears: Sikh tradition traces the sangat to Guru Nanak's time; the Rehras shabads themselves keep pointing to the satsangat as the means of crossing over.
